questions.q: The number of molecules in $22$ g of $\text{CO}_{2}$ is:
questions.solution:
$n = \dfrac{22}{44} = 0.5$ mol, so the number of molecules is $0.5 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = \mathbf{3.01 \times 10^{23}}$.

Always convert mass to **moles** first; the Avogadro constant then does the rest.

questions.q: The maximum number of electrons in a sub-shell with $l = 2$ is:
questions.solution:
$l = 2$ is the **d** sub-shell, with five orbitals holding two electrons each — $\mathbf{10}$.

In general the capacity is $2(2l + 1)$: s $2$, p $6$, d $10$, f $14$.

questions.q: The hybridisation of carbon in ethene is:
questions.solution:
Each carbon forms three $\sigma$ bonds and is therefore $\mathbf{sp^{2}}$ hybridised, with a leftover $p$ orbital forming the $\pi$ bond.

The molecule is **planar** with $120°$ angles, and the $\pi$ bond is what locks the geometry and gives E-Z isomerism.

questions.q: For a spontaneous process at constant temperature and pressure:
questions.solution:
$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, and a process is spontaneous when $\Delta G$ is **negative**.

An endothermic reaction can still be spontaneous if $\Delta S$ is large enough — which is why ammonium nitrate dissolves while cooling its own solution.

questions.q: For $\text{N}_{2} + 3\text{H}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_{3}$, increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium:
questions.solution:
There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium **right**, towards fewer molecules.

Le Chatelier's principle: the system acts to relieve the imposed pressure.

questions.q: The pH of $0.001$ M HCl is:
A buffer solution of pH $9$ can be made from:
questions.solution:
A **basic** buffer is needed for pH 9, so a weak base with its salt: $\text{NH}_{4}\text{OH}/\text{NH}_{4}\text{Cl}$.

The ethanoic acid buffer works near pH $4.7$, its $\text{p}K_{a}$. A strong acid with its salt is not a buffer at all.

questions.q: During the electrolysis of molten NaCl, the product at the cathode is:
questions.solution:
Reduction always occurs at the **cathode**, and in the molten salt the only cation present is $\text{Na}^{+}$:

$\text{Na}^{+} + e^{-} \to \text{Na}$

In **aqueous** solution the answer would be hydrogen instead, because water is easier to reduce than sodium ions.

questions.q: The half-life of a first order reaction:
questions.solution:
$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$ — **no** concentration term.

A constant half-life is the signature of first order kinetics, and it is why radioactive decay is described the same way.
options: is independent of the initial concentration

questions.q: Which of these is **not** a colligative property?
questions.solution:
Colligative properties depend only on the **number** of solute particles. **Optical rotation** depends entirely on the identity and structure of the molecule.

The four colligative properties are relative lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.

questions.q: The van't Hoff factor for $\text{K}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$, assuming complete dissociation, is:
questions.solution:
$\text{K}_{2}\text{SO}_{4} \to 2\text{K}^{+} + \text{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ — **three** particles from one formula unit, so $i = \mathbf{3}$.

That triples every colligative effect compared with an equal concentration of a non-electrolyte.

questions.q: Physisorption differs from chemisorption in that it:
questions.solution:
**Physisorption** relies on weak van der Waals forces: low enthalpy (about $20$ kJ/mol), **reversible**, and it **decreases** with rising temperature.

**Chemisorption** forms real chemical bonds, is largely irreversible, and needs an activation energy — so it first increases with temperature.
options: is reversible and has low enthalpy

questions.q: The number of atoms per unit cell in a face-centred cubic lattice is:
questions.solution:
Corners: $8 \times \tfrac18 = 1$. Faces: $6 \times \tfrac12 = 3$. Total $= \mathbf{4}$.

A simple cubic cell has 1 and a body-centred cubic cell has 2. Counting the shares correctly is the whole calculation.

questions.q: The oxidation number of chromium in $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$ is:
questions.solution:
$2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 2x = 12 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+6}$.

That high oxidation state is why dichromate is such a useful oxidising agent, and why it turns green ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$) as it is reduced.

questions.q: At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is halved. Its pressure:
questions.solution:
Boyle's law, $pV = $ constant, so the pressure **doubles**.

Microscopically: the molecules hit each square metre of wall twice as often, while their speed is unchanged because the temperature is.
